sentences.text: Adult individuals reached lengths of approximately 7 to 7.7 meters and masses ranging from 2.6 to 3.4 tonnes.
These animals possessed long limbs and a deep tail, allowing them to move on two or four legs.
Skin impressions reveal that their bodies were covered entirely in unornamented scales.
Modern research suggests their distinctive hollow cranial crest functioned as a resonating device for vocalization and identification.
William A. Parks formally named the genus Lambeosaurus in 1923.
The type species designated for this group is Lambeosaurus lambei.
Sternberg later described two additional species, L. magnicristatus and L. clavinitialis, in 1935.
As herbivores, they typically walked on four legs but could stand upright on their hind limbs.
Footprint evidence indicates that these creatures exhibited gregarious behavior.
They were fast animals, relying on speed and their large size as primary defenses against predators.
This genus serves as the eponymous member of the subfamily Lambeosaurinae and the tribe Lambeosaurini.
Recognized subdivisions include L. magnicristatus and the doubtful L. paucidens.
Several names, including Didanodon, Procheneosaurus, and Tetragonosaurus, are listed as synonyms of Lambeosaurus.
Lambeosaurus lived during the Campanian stage, spanning from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
Fossils are known only from the middle Campanian of the Dinosaur Park Formation in Alberta.
They inhabited a coastal plain featuring meandering rivers, dense conifer and fern vegetation, and diverse invertebrates, fish, mammals, and reptiles.
It is now known that a skull and skeleton previously thought to belong to the same individual were found 6 miles apart.
William J. Morris argued that very little separates Lambeosaurus, Corythosaurus, and Hypacrosaurus beyond skull anatomy, making identification of non-skull material difficult.
David B. Norman and Hans-Dieter Sues argued that Jaxartosaurus was too distinct in time and space from Procheneosaurus convincens to be assigned to any known genus.
David C. Evans and colleagues found that the type specimen of Tetragonosaurus cranibrevis showed Lambeosaurus anatomy, making it a synonym of Lambeosaurus instead of Corythosaurus.
